name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q01 - Carrier protein facilitated diffusion transport mechanisms

questiontext.text: Identify the transport mechanisms labelled X, Y, and Z in the given schematic of carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion across a biological membrane.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a biological membrane with three distinct carrier proteins labelled X, Y, and Z transporting molecules P and Q across the membrane:
- At X: Only molecule P moves across the membrane from left to right.
- At Y: Molecule P moves from left to right while molecule Q simultaneously moves from right to left.
- At Z: Both molecules P and Q move together from left to right.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All three mechanisms represent passive carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion occurring down a concentration gradient, classified by the number of transported species and their relative directions of movement.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Uniport: A single type of molecule moves across the membrane independently of other molecules.
- Antiport: Two types of molecules cross the membrane simultaneously in opposite directions.
- Symport: Two types of molecules cross the membrane together in the same direction.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Since carrier X transports only molecule P independently, X represents uniport.
2. Since carrier Y transports molecules P and Q in opposite directions, Y represents antiport.
3. Since carrier Z transports molecules P and Q together in the same direction, Z represents symport.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The directional arrows match the definitions of uniport (single arrow), antiport (opposing arrows), and symport (parallel arrows in the same direction). Therefore, X is uniport, Y is antiport, and Z is symport.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q02 - Water potential and osmosis between adjacent cells

questiontext.text: Two adjacent plant cells, P and Q, separated by a selectively permeable membrane, have solute potentials (\(\Psi_s\)) and pressure potentials (\(\Psi_p\)) as shown in the diagram. What will be the net direction of water movement and the water potential (\(\Psi_w\)) of cell P?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the diagram, two adjacent cells P and Q are separated by a selectively permeable membrane:
- For cell P: solute potential \(\Psi_s(P) = -1200\text{ kPa}\), pressure potential \(\Psi_p(P) = +400\text{ kPa}\).
- For cell Q: solute potential \(\Psi_s(Q) = -1800\text{ kPa}\), pressure potential \(\Psi_p(Q) = +500\text{ kPa}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Solute potential \(\Psi_s\) is negative, and positive turgor pressure gives a positive pressure potential \(\Psi_p\). Water moves by osmosis from the system with a higher (less negative) water potential to the system with a lower (more negative) water potential.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The water potential of a plant cell is given by:
\[\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate the water potential of cell P:
\[\Psi_w(P) = -1200\text{ kPa} + 400\text{ kPa} = -800\text{ kPa}\]
2. Calculate the water potential of cell Q:
\[\Psi_w(Q) = -1800\text{ kPa} + 500\text{ kPa} = -1300\text{ kPa}\]
3. Compare the two water potentials:
Since \(-800\text{ kPa} > -1300\text{ kPa}\), cell P has a higher water potential than cell Q.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are consistent in kilopascals (\(\text{kPa}\)), and water flows down the water potential gradient from higher (\(-800\text{ kPa}\)) to lower (\(-1300\text{ kPa}\)). Thus, the net movement of water is from cell P to cell Q, and the water potential of cell P is \(-800\text{ kPa}\).

answer.text: From Q to P; \(\Psi_w\) of P is \(-1600\text{ kPa}\)
From P to Q; \(\Psi_w\) of P is \(-1600\text{ kPa}\)
From P to Q; \(\Psi_w\) of P is \(-800\text{ kPa}\)
From Q to P; \(\Psi_w\) of P is \(-800\text{ kPa}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q03 - Apoplast and symplast water pathways in root

questiontext.text: In the given schematic showing the pathway of water movement through root layers, identify the impermeable barrier labelled X in the endodermis and the pathway labelled Y that moves water through adjacent cell walls in the cortex.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic depicts four concentric root layers—Epidermis, Cortex, Endodermis, and Pericycle—leading to the Xylem. Label X indicates a dark vertical band embedded in the radial/transverse walls of the endodermis, and Pathway Y follows the continuous cell wall system from the epidermis through the cortex until it is deflected into the endodermal cytoplasm just before X.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Water movement in roots occurs via two distinct routes: through the non-living cell wall continuum or through the living interconnected protoplasts.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- The apoplast is the system of adjacent cell walls continuous throughout the plant, except at the Casparian strip of the root endodermis.
- The Casparian strip is a band of suberised matrix that is impervious to water, forcing water to cross the plasma membrane and enter the symplast at the endodermis.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Structure X blocks water movement through the cell wall at the endodermis; therefore, X is the Casparian strip.
2. Pathway Y travels exclusively through the cell walls and intercellular spaces of the epidermis and cortex without crossing a membrane until reaching the endodermis; therefore, Y is the apoplast pathway.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This matches the physiological requirement that water movement through root layers is ultimately symplastic in the endodermis due to the suberised Casparian strip. Hence, X is the Casparian strip and Y is the apoplast pathway.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q04 - Pressure flow hypothesis of phloem translocation

questiontext.text: The diagram illustrates the pressure flow hypothesis of sugar translocation in phloem from a source leaf to a sink root. Which of the following correctly identifies the processes occurring at arrows 1, 2, 3, and 4?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows adjacent Xylem and Phloem columns connected to a Source (leaf cell) at the top and a Sink (root cell) at the bottom. Arrows 1 and 3 indicate sugar movement at the source and sink, respectively, while arrows 2 and 4 indicate water movement between xylem and phloem at the source and sink, respectively.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Translocation in the phloem follows the pressure flow (mass flow) hypothesis, driven by hydrostatic pressure gradients created by osmotic water movement.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Loading sucrose into companion cells and sieve tubes at the source requires metabolic energy (active transport), producing a hypertonic condition.
- Water moves by osmosis from regions of higher water potential (xylem) to lower water potential (hypertonic phloem), building hydrostatic pressure.
- Unloading sucrose at the sink also requires active transport, raising the water potential in the phloem so water exits by osmosis.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. At arrow 1 (source to phloem): Sucrose is moved into the sieve tube by active loading of sucrose.
2. At arrow 2 (xylem to phloem at source): Due to the hypertonic condition in the phloem, there is osmotic entry of water from the adjacent xylem.
3. At arrow 3 (phloem to sink): Sucrose is moved out of the phloem into sink cells by active unloading of sucrose.
4. At arrow 4 (phloem to xylem at sink): Loss of solute increases the water potential in the phloem, resulting in osmotic exit of water back to the xylem.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This sequence maintains high turgor pressure at the source and low turgor pressure at the sink, driving bulk flow from source to sink. Therefore, 1 is active loading of sucrose, 2 is osmotic entry of water, 3 is active unloading of sucrose, and 4 is osmotic exit of water.

answer.text: 1 = Passive loading of sucrose, 2 = Osmotic exit of water, 3 = Active unloading of sucrose, 4 = Osmotic entry of water
1 = Active loading of sucrose, 2 = Active transport of water, 3 = Passive unloading of sucrose, 4 = Osmotic exit of water
1 = Active loading of sucrose, 2 = Osmotic exit of water, 3 = Active unloading of sucrose, 4 = Osmotic entry of water
1 = Active loading of sucrose, 2 = Osmotic entry of water, 3 = Active unloading of sucrose, 4 = Osmotic exit of water
